lens:
EMPIRICAL ASSET PRICING: price pressure versus information, conditioned on the fear model's shock type.

The fear model provides four things the families use:
- the systemic/idiosyncratic day label;
- the own-sigma yardstick (sigma, x);
- the stress level (M_pct);
- the filtered state probabilities and transition matrix.

Together these separate two kinds of move:
- (a) Non-informational selling on broad fear days. Liquidity providers are paid to absorb it, and paid more when stress is high (Nagel 2012).
- (b) Firm-specific news. The market under-prices it when a market-wide shock consumes attention (Peng & Xiong 2006; Hirshleifer, Lim & Teoh 2009).

Z and I are deliberately not used as entry signals. They are HMM-smoothed, with a memory of about 14 sessions, so they mix recent news with today's displacement.

Both families are cross-sectional and long-only. Both are judged against the beta-adjusted equal-weight AI basket plus a same-stock baseline, so market timing never enters. That is how they differ from the tests that failed:
- M predicting basket returns: Hodrick t 0.70.
- Buying Z >= 2.5 versus the same stock on random days. That test used raw returns and pooled systemic with idiosyncratic panics. Its sign flip between 2023-25 and 2026 is what a beta-dominated payoff that depends on the market's path would produce.

Priority: A first. Test B only if the budget allows a second family from this lens.

Deliberately not proposed, to save multiple-testing budget:
- (i) Idiosyncratic no-news reversal. Only about 104 dev events, a weak price-only news proxy, and Nagel's own theory predicts a small liquidity premium in calm markets.
- (ii) Bearish news drift through long puts. The plausible drift in liquid AI names, about 1-2%, is below put theta plus the variance premium plus 3-10% spreads (Coval & Shumway 2001; Bakshi & Kapadia 2003). There is no IV history to test it.
- (iii) IVOL, MAX/lottery and betting-against-beta. Their payoff sits in the short leg (Stambaugh, Yu & Yuan 2015), and the hindsight-selected AI-winner universe biases them.
- (iv) Momentum crashes (Daniel & Moskowitz 2016) and volatility-managed basket timing (Moreira & Muir 2017). Both are market-level, with 4-8 episodes, so no power in two years (Cederburg et al. 2020).

All event counts below come from same-day and trailing signal data only: x, the systemic label, same-day returns, gaps and volume. No post-event return was computed. Script: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-fear-signal/746ee66c-3d9a-5a30-89ca-deab40db82a0/scratchpad/event_counts3.py. Nothing was written in the repository.

families.name: A. Systemic-shock liquidity-provision reversal (segment- and beta-adjusted, news-filtered)
families.mechanism:
Liquidity provision under stress, applied to the residual of a broad AI fear day.

On a systemic day (the fear model's label: at least 10% of eligible stocks dip at least 2 own-sigma below the previous close), much of the selling is non-informational: de-grossing of crowded AI longs, thematic and leveraged-ETF flows, volatility-target and margin-driven sales.

Liquidity providers absorb it. They demand a premium that rises with market stress, because their capital and risk-bearing capacity shrink:
- Nagel 2012 RFS: reversal profits rise with VIX.
- Hameed, Kang & Viswanathan 2010 JF: reversals are larger after market declines.
- Campbell, Grossman & Wang 1993 QJE.
- Brunnermeier & Pedersen 2009 RFS.
- Barrot, Kaniel & Sraer 2016 JFE: retail liquidity provision earns more when VIX is high.

Capital arrives slowly, so the reversal plays out over days (Duffie 2010 JF; Mitchell, Pedersen & Pulvino 2007 AER).

After removing beta and the segment move, what is left of a stock's hit is mostly flow exposure, which reverses. The segment and news components carry information:
- Hameed & Mian 2015 JFQA.
- Da, Liu & Schaumburg 2014 Management Science.
- Engelberg, Gao & Jagannathan 2009 WP: pairs divergences after common news or liquidity shocks converge; those after idiosyncratic news do not.
- Ben-David, Franzoni & Moussawi 2018 JF and Coval & Stafford 2007 JFE: non-fundamental flow shocks.

Stocks whose drop came with firm-specific overnight news are removed, because news-driven moves drift rather than reverse (Chan 2003 JFE; Savor 2012 JFE; Tetlock 2010 RFS).

Horizon caveat: high-turnover stocks show short-term momentum at one month (Medhat & Schmeling 2022 RFS). The premium is therefore expected over days to two weeks only.
families.entry_rule:
At the close of t, using only fear outputs and prices up to t:

(1) Day: t is a fear-model systemic day (the share of eligible stocks with x >= 2 is at least 10%) and not an NYSE early-close session, which reads artificially quiet.

(2) Stock eligibility: fear-model eligible; close_t >= $5; median(close x volume) over t-20..t-1 >= $20M; not already held by this family.

(3) Fear participation: x_i,t >= 2.

(4) Residual displacement:
- r_B,t = equal-weight mean of r over eligible stocks.
- beta_i = (2/3) x OLS slope of r_i on r_B over t-126..t-1 (at least 100 observations) + 1/3.
- u_i,t = (r_i,t - beta_i x r_B,t) / sigma_i,t, with sigma from the fear model.
- v_i,t = u_i,t minus the median u of eligible stocks in i's segment that day (the all-stock median if the segment has fewer than 3 eligible).
- Require v_i,t <= -1.5.

(5) News filter:
- gamma_i,t = ln(adjusted open_t / adjusted close_t-1) / sigma_i,t.
- g_i,t = gamma_i,t minus the segment median gamma.
- Exclude g_i,t <= -2. An idiosyncratic overnight gap means likely earnings or other firm news.

(6) Cap: if more than 10 stocks qualify, keep the 10 with the most negative v.
families.execution:
Entry: the systemic label and x are final only after the close of t, so buy at the official open of t+1 with market-on-open orders.

Test portfolio, used for every selection test: calendar-time, equal weight across all open events each session (Fama 1998). Daily excess = mean over open events of (r_i - beta_i x r_B). Costs are charged on entry and exit days.

Live sleeve: split into H staggered tranches (Jegadeesh & Titman 1993), one per event day, with equal weight inside the cohort. Caps are under sizing.

Delay test: buy at the open of t+2 and exit H sessions later.
families.exit_rule:
Sell at the open of t+1+H (H = 5; H = 10 for A2).

Time exit only: no stop-loss and no profit target. A stock that re-qualifies while held is not added, and its clock does not reset.

CSP version: hold to the chosen expiry, or buy back at 75% of maximum profit. If assigned, sell the shares at the next open.
variants: A1 (primary): rule as stated, H = 5 sessions.
A2: as A1 with H = 10 sessions (slow-moving capital).
A3: as A1, only on event days with point-in-time M_pct_t >= 1.0 (Nagel's stress dose).

A4: as A1 but beta-only. Steps 4 and 6 use u <= -1.5 instead of v, and the news gap is gamma minus the all-stock median gamma. This tests whether the segment component also reverses, for example under thematic-ETF flows.
families.benchmark:
Per event, the beta-adjusted excess over the identical window: e = R_i - beta_i x R_B.
- R is the open(t+1) to open(t+1+H) total return; R_B is the equal-weight mean of the same-window returns of all eligible stocks.
- beta_i is the trailing shrunk beta used in the signal.
- The stock leg is charged 10 bps per side (stress test 25 bps).

Inference: stationary bootstrap (mean block about 10 sessions) on the calendar-time daily excess series. This respects the clustering of systemic days.

The excess must also stay positive against a same-stock baseline: e minus stock i's mean e over all its dev sessions at the same H. This removes the hindsight drift of AI winners.
families.predicted_signature:
Required:
- (R1) Mean net excess > 0, about +0.5% to +1.5% per event. That is 0.2-0.6 own-sigma, or 10-30% of the median 2.0-sigma residual displacement. It should accrue mostly in sessions 1-5, with at least half still present at session 20: a pressure reversal, not noise or a passing risk premium.
- (R2) Stress dose: event excess rises with M_pct_t (positive slope, standard errors clustered by day), and A3 >= A1.
- (R3) Shock-type contrast: the identical rule on idiosyncratic days (about 499 dev events) earns less than on systemic days.
- (R4) The intercept of event excess regressed on the holding-window basket return stays > 0, so the gain is not a realized-beta artefact of a market rebound.

Supporting:
- The news-excluded systemic-day set (g <= -2, about 133 dev events) earns less; it drifts.
- The most displaced tercile (v <= -2.3) beats the least displaced (v > -1.8).
- The effect is larger in the less liquid half.
- At least half the excess survives the one-day delay.
- The sign survives leaving out any one of the 25 clusters.
- If A4 beats A1, the gain concentrates in compute, semicap and foundry/memory, where ETF flows are heaviest.
families.expected_events_2024_2025:
Counts use same-day signal data only; no outcome was looked at.

Dev period: 127 systemic days (25% of sessions), forming 25 clusters separated by more than 5 sessions and 12 by more than 10.
- A1: about 535 stock-events on 124 days, about 4.3 names per day. Median own sigma 2.3%/day, median beta 0.91. Spread over all eight quarters, 29-113 per quarter.
- A2: slightly fewer, because re-qualifications within 10 sessions are not re-entered.
- A3: about 232 events on 44 days.
- A4: about 725 events on 126 days.

2026 holdout: A1 about 329 events on 75 days (9 clusters); A3 about 142 on 35 days.

Power:
- The 5-day residual s.d. is about 6% per event and about 3.5-4.5% per daily cohort, with roughly 60-80 effectively independent cohorts.
- A true net mean of +1.0% per event gives t of about 2-2.5; +0.6% gives about 1.2-1.5.
- Moderate: it needs about 0.4 own-sigma of reversal to clear SPA plus Holm.
- That is still far more power than the market-level M >= 2 test (4 episodes).
families.options_expression:
Default: shares.

Use a cash-secured put instead when options are rich relative to the fear model's forward volatility:
- rho = IV_ATM(expiry nearest H) / sigma_fwd.
- sigma_fwd = sigma_i x sqrt(252) x sqrt(mean over h = 1..H of sum_k (alpha_t A^h)_k s_k^2), using the filtered state probabilities and the current point-in-time transition matrix A and scales s.
- Condition: rho >= 1.25, bid-ask <= 5% of mid, open interest >= 500.
- Then sell a put at the first expiry at least H sessions away, strike nearest -0.40 delta, fully cash-secured.

Why a CSP:
- It keeps the stress-inflated premium. Variance premia peak in stress (Bollerslev, Tauchen & Zhou 2009; Carr & Wu 2009). Option-demand pressure raises prices (Garleanu, Pedersen & Poteshman 2009). Options rich against realized volatility earn low returns for buyers (Goyal & Saretto 2009).
- It earns roughly half the reversal through delta.
- Assignment means buying below the entry price.

When options beat shares: rho is high and the expected reversal in % is below the premium. Shares win in a sharp, fast rebound, because the CSP caps the upside.

No long calls: IV is at its richest on systemic days, and stressed losers already carry call-like convexity (Daniel & Moskowitz 2016).

Validation: spend about 20 of the ~30 retrievable expired-contract samples on A events, stratified by M_pct, to compare CSP and share P&L net of spreads. This checks the implementation; it is not a selection test.
families.main_risks:
(1) Overnight reversal: part of the reversal happens overnight (leveraged-ETF closing pressure: Cheng & Madhavan 2009). Next-open entry, and the one-day delay test, may lose it.

(2) Falling knives: systemic days cluster. Buying day-one losers inside a multi-week drawdown loses money before liquidity returns (liquidity spirals). With only 25 clusters, one episode can dominate.

(3) Beta drift: betas rise in crises (Ang & Chen 2002), so u can mislabel high-beta names as displaced. R4 and the segment adjustment guard against this.

(4) Hidden news: segment-specific news on a systemic day (export controls, a hyperscaler capex guide) can look like flow. The overnight-gap filter misses news released during the session.

(5) Hindsight universe: names that crashed and never recovered are missing, which biases the reversal upward. The same-stock baseline only partly fixes this.

(6) Costs: about 535 round trips. At 25 bps per side the hurdle is 0.5% per event.

(7) Short-term momentum in high-turnover stocks (Medhat & Schmeling 2022) may offset the reversal beyond 10 sessions.

(8) Unhedged beta: the sleeve holds about 1x basket beta through stress drawdowns, and the long-only constraints rule out hedging.

families.name: B. Good news in bad times: distraction drift after positive news on systemic fear days
families.mechanism:
In bad times, limited attention goes to the aggregate shock.

When the market is absorbed by a systemic fear shock, investors and fund managers shift attention to market-wide information and under-process firm-specific news:
- Peng & Xiong 2006 JFE.
- Peng, Xiong & Bollerslev 2007 European Financial Management.
- Kacperczyk, Van Nieuwerburgh & Veldkamp 2016 Econometrica: attention moves to aggregate shocks when aggregate volatility is high.

Firm news released on such days is under-priced on the day and drifts afterwards:
- Hirshleifer, Lim & Teoh 2009 JF: distracting days.
- DellaVigna & Pollet 2009 JF: Friday announcements.
- Kottimukkalur 2019 JFQA: underreaction to earnings on market-moving days.
- Veronesi 1999 RFS: underreaction to good news in bad times.

News-driven moves continue rather than reverse (Chan 2003 JFE; Pritamani & Singal 2001 JBF; Jiang & Zhu 2017 JFE; Jiang, Li & Wang 2021 JFE).

The price-only footprint of good news on a fear day: a stock rises at least 1 own-sigma, sits at least 2 own-sigma above its segment's beta-implied move, and trades on abnormal volume, while the fear model says the market is in a systemic dip.

The fear model supplies the bad-times label and the own-sigma yardstick. Taking the bullish side keeps the trade long-only.
families.entry_rule:
At the close of t:

(1) Day: t is a fear-model systemic day and not an NYSE early-close session (half-day volume and ranges read artificially quiet).

(2) Eligibility and liquidity: as in A; not already held by this family.

(3) Residual: v_i,t >= +2, the same segment- and beta-adjusted residual as A, in own sigmas.

(4) Absolute gain: r_i,t >= +1 x sigma_i,t, at least one own-sigma up on a broad fear day.

(5) News proxy: abnormal volume, volume_t / median(volume over t-20..t-1) >= 2 (Chan 2003; Pritamani & Singal 2001).
families.execution:
Entry: buy at the official open of t+1 with market-on-open orders.

Test portfolio, used for every selection test: calendar-time, equal weight across all open events each session. Daily excess is measured against beta times the basket; costs are charged on entry and exit days.

Live: each event gets a fixed allocation of 1/15 of the B sleeve, about 6 concurrent on average at H = 20. If the sleeve is full the event is skipped and logged.

Delay test: buy at the open of t+2.
families.exit_rule:
Sell at the open of t+1+H (H = 20; H = 40 for B2).

Time exit only: no stops, and no re-entry while held.

Option versions: calls are sold at the same time exit and never held to expiry. CSPs are held to expiry or bought back at 75% of maximum profit; assigned shares are sold at the next open.
variants: B1 (primary): rule as stated, H = 20 sessions.
B2: as B1 with H = 40 sessions, closer to the 60-day PEAD window.
B3: as B1 with stronger news, v >= +3.
B4: as B1 without the abnormal-volume condition: a pure price footprint with more events.
families.benchmark:
Same construction as A: per-event e = R_i - beta_i x R_B over the identical open(t+1) to open(t+1+H) window against the equal-weight AI basket. The stock leg is charged 10 bps per side (stress test 25 bps).

Inference: stationary bootstrap on the calendar-time daily excess series.

The excess must also beat the same-stock baseline: e minus stock i's mean e over all its dev sessions at the same H. This matters more for B than for A, because good-news events are where the AI-winner hindsight bias concentrates.
families.predicted_signature:
Required:
- (R1) Mean net excess > 0, about +1.5% to +3% at 20 sessions, accruing gradually. It should stay positive when the first post-entry session is excluded, with at least 40% of it arriving after session 5: a drift, not a one-day pop.
- (R2) Distraction contrast: the identical rule on idiosyncratic days, where attention is not diverted (about 540 dev events), earns less.
- (R3) The intercept of event excess regressed on the holding-window basket return stays > 0.

Supporting:
- Excess rises with M_pct_t on the event day.
- The overnight-news subset (g >= +1, about 105 dev events; scheduled releases outside market hours) drifts at least as much as the rest.
- B3 >= B1 (dose).
- B2 adds to B1 rather than reversing it.
families.expected_events_2024_2025:
Counts use same-day signal data only.

Dev period:
- B1: about 160 events on 74 systemic days, 89 distinct tickers. Event-day M_pct quartiles -0.02, 0.41, 1.36. Only 2 events in 2025Q2.
- B2: about 160, less re-qualifications.
- B3: about 105.
- B4: about 261 on 98 days.
- Contrast set on idiosyncratic days: about 540.

2026 holdout: B1 about 89, B3 44, B4 158.

Power:
- Events are largely independent firm news, so effective N is close to the count. But the 20-day residual s.d. is about 11-13% per event.
- A true +2.5% gives t of about 2.2; +1.5% gives about 1.3.
- Low-to-moderate power. The 2026 holdout alone can confirm only drifts of about 3% or more.
families.options_expression:
Use the same rho = IV_ATM / sigma_fwd, here at 45-60 DTE. After earnings, IV is usually crushed.

- rho <= 1.0 (options cheap against the stock's own forward volatility; low-IV options earn more, Goyal & Saretto 2009): buy 45-60 DTE calls near 0.60 delta. Size them to the share position's delta, with premium <= 1% of capital per trade. This gives defined risk and convexity to continued drift.
- rho >= 1.25 (non-earnings news keeps IV rich): sell a 30-45 DTE cash-secured put near -0.30 delta. It collects the variance premium and profits if the drift merely holds.
- Otherwise: buy shares.

Require bid-ask <= 5% of mid and open interest >= 500.

Calls beat shares only when IV sits below forward realized volatility and the drift is a few percent. At fair IV, theta absorbs a 2% drift.

Never use covered calls here: they sell the upside the family predicts.

Validation: spend about 10 of the ~30 expired-contract samples on B events to check this rule.
families.main_risks:
(1) Hindsight selection: names with good news that went on to become 2026 AI winners are in the universe by construction. B is the family most exposed to this look-ahead bias, and the 2026 holdout shares it, so only the prospective paper test is clean.

(2) Weak drift: large-cap PEAD has largely disappeared (Martineau 2022; Chordia et al. 2009), and AI names get intense attention, so the drift may be near zero.

(3) Mixed events dilute the drift. Index inclusions partly reverse (Harris & Gurel 1986). M&A targets go flat. Attention-driven retail spikes reverse (Barber & Odean 2008; Seasholes & Wu 2007).

(4) Low power and seasonality: events cluster in earnings seasons, and 20-40 session windows contain sector reports.

(5) Untested options rule: historical option IV after news is unknown, so the option rule rests on about 10 contract samples.

position_sizing_and_risk:
Cash account, no margin, long-only, level-2 options.

Selection tests use the unconstrained calendar-time event portfolios declared in each family. The sleeve rules below are the live implementation. They are also simulated on dev and 2026 as a reported check, never as a selection input.

(1) Sleeves
- A: at most 50% of trading capital. B: at most 30%. The rest stays cash, which also secures CSP assignments.
- Each sleeve carries about 1x AI-basket beta in stress, so size the total for a 25-30% basket drawdown.

(2) Allocation and caps
- A: H staggered tranches (Jegadeesh & Titman 1993), one per event day, equal weight within the cohort, at most 10 names.
- B: 1/15 of the sleeve per event.
- Caps: at most 5% of capital in any single A position and 4% in any B position; at most 40% of a cohort in one segment.
- Each order at most 1% of the stock's 20-day median dollar volume, via market-on-open.

(3) No stop-losses
Both payoffs are bounded by their horizon, and stops on mean-reverting positions sell at the worst prices (Kaminski & Lo 2014). Exits are by time only.

(4) Fear-model risk monitor
Reported daily; it is not a trading signal. Expected next-day tail loss = sum over positions of w_i x q_next_i x 3 x sigma_i. If it exceeds 2% of capital, new cohorts are scaled down pro rata. This is a fixed rule, applied in the simulated check too.

(5) Options
- CSPs are fully cash-secured inside their tranche: contracts = floor(cash / (100 x strike)); if that is zero, use shares.
- Call premium at most 1% of capital per trade and 3% in total.
- No covered calls on A or B positions.

(6) Governance
- Pre-register a sequential guard for the paper test: after every 25 closed events, suspend a family whose running net excess is below its dev estimate minus 2 s.e.
- Account circuit breaker: no new cohorts while equity is more than 15% below its peak; resume once it is back within 10%.

(7) Conviction tiers for the daily output
- High conviction requires all of: the family passed every gate, 2026 agreed, and the event is in its dev top dose tercile.
  - A: v <= -2.3, plus M_pct_t >= 1 if the stress-dose signature held.
  - B: v >= +4.4.
- Standard: other events of an adopted family.
- A family that was not adopted is display-only and never traded.

Each output row lists: ticker, family and variant, entry open date, exit date, instrument (shares, or CSP or calls with strike and expiry), size, tier, and the fear inputs that triggered it (systemic flag, x, v, g, M_pct, rho).
